← Landscape lighting bid calculator

How much to charge to install landscape lighting

Landscape lighting contractors get shopped on a published $150 a light installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the trench or the transformer. Six path lights on an existing transformer is a different job from an 18-fixture architectural install with well lights, a new 300W transformer, irrigated-turf trench, and a driveway saw-cut.

Open the free landscape lighting bid calculator

Price the fixtures and the trench, not the $150 dump

Landscape lighting is a fixture mix, then a scope, then how you get power there. Path lights are a stake. Uplights are aim and a spike. Well lights are a dig and a drain. Fixtures-only hangs lights on a transformer that is already there. A new system is trench, low-voltage wire, and a transformer. An add-on is a home-run back to what is already on the house.

Fixtures-only is not a new system

The cheap special is almost always path lights on an existing transformer, no trench, no wells, no saw-cut. A new-system architectural job is a different crew day. Matching a per-light number on a new-system yard is how a sold lighting job becomes a loss when the home-run and the well lights eat the margin.

This is not holiday lights or an electrical panel

Holiday lights are a seasonal C9 hang and January take-down. An electrical panel is service amps. Irrigation install is water zones and a backflow. Exterior painting is a coat on elevations. This prices landscape lighting: fixtures, trench, transformer, and extras. The trench here is a low-voltage home-run, not those other jobs.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the landscape lighting bid calculator. It is not an electrical design, a load calculation, a voltage-drop study, a permit determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install landscape lighting?

Charge from fixture mix, scope, trench, soil, and extras — not a published $150 / light special. Six path lights on an existing transformer is a different job from an 18-fixture architectural install with well lights, a new transformer, irrigated-turf trench, and a driveway saw-cut.

Is fixtures-only the same bid as a new landscape lighting system?

No. Fixtures-only hangs lights on a transformer and wire that are already there. A new system is a trench, low-voltage wire, and a transformer. An add-on is a home-run back to what is already on the house. Matching a per-light special on a new-system job is how a sold lighting job becomes a loss when the trench eats the margin.

How do well lights and trench change a landscape lighting price?

A path light is a stake. A well light is a dig and a drain. Trench lineal feet, irrigated turf repair, rocky soil, a photocell, a driveway saw-cut, and a second transformer do not live in a published per-light dump.

Is this the same as holiday lights or an electrical panel?

No. Holiday lights are a seasonal C9 hang and January take-down. An electrical panel is service amps. Irrigation install is water zones and a backflow. This prices landscape lighting: fixtures, trench, transformer, and extras.

    Common questions

    Why is my price so much higher than a $150-a-light quote I saw?

    A flat per-light number usually assumes the cheapest scenario in this tool: fixtures-only on an existing transformer, easy soil, no trench. Switching to a new-system job adds trench footage, wire, and a transformer that a per-fixture rate cannot see. Use the “Same yard, three scopes” comparison to see exactly how much of the gap is trench and transformer.

    What is the difference between the fixtures-only, new-system, and existing-add-on presets?

    Fixtures-only assumes you are hanging lights on a transformer that is already there — no trench, no wire run. New-system assumes you are trenching, running wire, and installing a transformer from scratch. Existing-add-on assumes a shorter home-run trench back into a system already on the house. Picking the wrong one under- or over-fills your starting trench and transformer hours.

    Does the walk-away price include any profit for me?

    No. The walk-away price is your total cost with zero margin built in — labor, fixtures, wire, transformer, and overhead, but no profit. The price above it is the one that includes your target net margin; quoting at or below the walk-away number means the job cannot lose money, but it also cannot pay you.

    Do irrigated turf and rocky soil actually change the price, or just the hours?

    Both. Harder soil adds trenching hours at your loaded wage, and irrigated turf also adds a turf-repair material cost per lineal foot for the sod you disturb. Picking “easy” soil on a yard with an irrigation system underprices the trench twice — once in time, once in material.

vs-a-flat-150-per-light-special.html.text:
← Landscape Lighting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $150-a-light special

“$150 a light installed” is not a price for landscape lighting — it is a price for one specific fixture, scope, and soil, quietly applied to every yard that calls in.

What a flat price per light is

A flat rate per fixture is the fastest way to quote a lighting job: multiply the light count by a number and read off a price. It is the number a homeowner holding a Facebook special or a competitor's flyer will call and ask you to match, whatever their yard actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a handful of path lights on a transformer and wire that are already there, no trench, no new transformer, no wells — and then reused for every install afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter path, uplight, well, and hardscape fixture counts, trench length, scope (fixtures-only, new system, or an add-on), soil, transformer size, and extras like a photocell or a driveway saw-cut, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the trench, the transformer, and every fixture type separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this yard, not a generic one.

What a flat price per light doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/light whether the transformer and wire are already there or a new system needs trenching and a transformer, even though a new system adds trench hours, wire, and a transformer invoice no fixture count captures. Prices scope separately — fixtures-only, new-system, or add-on — so a job that needs a trench and a transformer costs more than one that reuses what is already installed.
Has no line for soil, regardless of whether the trench runs through easy sandy lawn or irrigated turf that needs a sod repair. Prices soil hours and turf-repair cost separately by soil kind, so an irrigated-turf trench costs more than a shovel trench through easy lawn.
Charges the same rate for a path stake as for a well light that needs a dig and a drain, or a hardscape fixture that needs fasteners on stone. Prices each fixture type's own hours and material cost separately, so a wells-and-hardscape job costs more than the same fixture count of path lights.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-light rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two yards, the same fixture-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($32/hr crew wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $121.38/light rateGap
6 path lights, existing transformer, no trench — the walkway special the rate is set from$728.26 bid price; $582.61 break-even cost$728.26 (exactly $121.38/light — this rate is fit to this job)No gap on the job the rate was built on.
20-fixture architectural install: 6 path, 8 uplights, 4 well lights, 2 hardscape, new 300W transformer, 180 LF trench through irrigated turf, driveway saw-cut$5,773.11 bid price; $4,618.49 break-even cost$2,427.53The rate quotes $2,190.96 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $3,345.58 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $121.38/light rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the walkway-special preset, divided by that preset's fixture count. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the wells-and-trench architectural job, it counts only the twenty fixtures and never sees the transformer, the trench, the irrigated-turf soil work, or the saw-cut at all. Run your own yard's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-light rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one yard it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per light get a landscape lighting bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is scope (fixtures-only on an existing transformer versus a new system with trench and a transformer versus an add-on home-run), soil (easy lawn versus irrigated turf versus rocky ground), the transformer size, and fixture type (a path stake versus a well light that needs a dig and a drain) -- not a blended fixture count. A twenty-fixture architectural install with wells, a new transformer, and 180 feet of trench through irrigated turf is doing several jobs a six-path-light walkway on an existing transformer never touches, none of which scale with the light count the way a per-light rate assumes.

What does a flat price per light usually leave out entirely?

Trench footage and the soil it runs through, a new or larger transformer, the difference between a path stake, an uplight, a well light, and a hardscape fastener, and extras like a photocell, an astronomic timer, or a driveway saw-cut. A six-light walkway on an existing transformer is doing far less than a twenty-fixture job with wells, trench, and a saw-cut -- and a per-light number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates: six path lights on an existing transformer -- the walkway special -- prices at $728.26, or $121.38 a fixture. Applying that same $121.38 rate to a twenty-fixture architectural install (wells, a new 300W transformer, 180 feet of trench through irrigated turf, and a driveway saw-cut) quotes $2,427.53 -- $2,190.96 below that job's own $4,618.49 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $3,345.58 below the calculator's own $5,773.11 bid price.

Is a flat price per light ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same scope, no trench, no new transformer, all path lights -- a per-light rate can land close, and on this calculator's own walkway-special preset it is exactly the rate that job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which yard it was built on and neither does the estimator until scope, soil, transformer, and fixture type are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the fixture counts by type, trench length, scope, soil, transformer size, and extras, plus the labor hours, fixture and material costs, and wage you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-light rate skips, not a market survey.

vs-aspire.html.text:
← Landscape Lighting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aspire

Two different shapes: Aspire is an account-based business-management platform for running a landscape company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this landscape-lighting job cost, given its fixtures and trenching — before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Aspire is a cloud business-management platform, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton, headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri. It is built for landscape maintenance and construction contractors, as well as irrigation, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning companies, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with a mobile app for crews in the field. Its own plans are tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold at one flat price, and no dollar figure for any plan is published on its site — pricing is reached by requesting a demo. Aspire's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact tier names or any dollar figure, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a business-management platform serving landscape construction, irrigation, snow and ice, and cleaning contractors, sold as a revenue-tiered subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Aspire appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Aspire does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's fixture count and type, trenching or existing-bed wire runs, transformer sizing, and low-voltage wire gauge and length, plus loaded crew cost, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the install price, the effective crew hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
